messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Ship Captain
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Prevention Rumination: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented, Past Dwelling: I dwell on how I used to be before the event, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down, Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Samira Haddad is a 53-year-old married woman who has spent much of her adult life at sea, where the routines of command, watch schedules, and constant attention to risk fit easily around a way of living that already felt organized around vigilance. She grew up in an Arab American household marked by physical abuse from a caregiver, and when she speaks about childhood she does not begin with a single story so much as a set of stark visual fragments: a hallway at night, the angle of a door partly open, a raised hand, the look of a room just before she knew she had to brace herself. At other times she can describe what happened in a flat, detached way that leaves her sounding to herself like she is talking about another girl entirely. What is striking to her is the inconsistency. Sometimes there are only pictures. Sometimes there is a factual account with no feeling in it. And sometimes there is no picture at all, only a sudden wave of terror and helplessness that feels exactly as strong as it did then.

As a child, what frightened Samira most was not only the abuse itself but the sense that nobody who should have noticed or intervened did so. Adults around her either failed to see it, failed to stop it, or failed to matter. She had come to believe early that the people and systems that were supposed to protect children had let her down. Over the years that conviction widened into something more general and more enduring: the world is dangerous, safety is provisional, and depending on protection from other people is a mistake. She also describes a quieter loss that has sat alongside this for years. She feels she has become separated from her community and culture, as though the parts of belonging that should have steadied her were thinned out long ago. She does not describe this dramatically; instead it appears in the way she talks about never quite feeling held by a larger circle, never fully at home in traditions that once might have been a refuge.

As she got older, Samira developed habits of mind that she experiences as relentless and exhausting. She dwells on how the abuse could have been prevented, replaying the circumstances and wondering which adult should have stepped in, what sign should have been recognized, what might have been different if someone had acted one day earlier. She also finds herself dwelling on who she was before those experiences shaped her life, imagining a version of herself who might have moved through the world with less hardness and less suspicion. At the same time, she tries hard not to think about the trauma at all. She keeps mental doors shut, redirects herself, and pushes away any thought that feels like it might lead further in. The effort is familiar to her and rarely successful for long.

Her work as a ship captain places her in environments where alertness is both professional and personal. On board, listening carefully is part of leadership and safety, but Samira notices that even at home on land she remains tuned for signs of intrusion. She listens for sounds that might mean someone is entering the house, especially after dark. A shift in the floorboards, a car door outside, a gate latch, the faint movement of someone in the hallway can pull her attention immediately. Night is always worse. Even when she knows she is safe, even when her husband is home and the doors are locked, her body will not settle. She finds it much harder to feel safe at night than during the day, as if darkness itself returns her to the expectancy of childhood, when danger approached from elsewhere in the house and being still was never the same as being secure. She cannot relax in safe places because the knowledge of safety does not feel persuasive enough to override what she senses and anticipates.

In recent months, the strain of living this way has become harder for her to dismiss. Long after a voyage ends, she remains keyed up in her own bedroom, listening. Her husband has noticed how often she checks sounds in the house and how distant she becomes when something stirs an emotional reaction she cannot fully name. She is worn down by the combination of intense feeling with no clear memory, visual snippets that arrive without warning, and stretches of numb recollection that make her feel alien to herself. Seeking help now, Samira says she is tired of living as though danger is always already at the threshold. What she fears most is that she will never experience rest, even in her own home. What she hopes for, cautiously, is not to forget, but to stop feeling that every night requires a watch.
